newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - Australia's Telstra says its no school bully.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Australia's Telstra says its no school bully.

text.p: Telstra Corp chief executive officer Frank Blount said on Tuesday that the group, which dominates Australia's A$15 billion telecommuncations industry, does not plan to be a "school bully" ahead of deregulation.
Nonetheless, Blount is confident of Telstra's pre-eminent position ahead of complete deregulation from July 1.
It will be better for the sector if competitors resolve industry issues themselves than in front of the regulator, he added.

"Some of you think we are by nature the archetypal school bully, prepared to use our size and strength to dominate our schoolyard," Blount told the Australian Telecommunications Users Group (ATUG) conference.

"I cannot convince some of you to see Telstra the way that I describe, simply by stating that that arrogance has no place in the new Telstra or anywhere else in the new era of communications," Blount said.

"That is why the relationships between us are so critical. Light-handed regulation will work much more effectively if we are to resolve our differences openly and honestly as they arrive," Blount said.

Telecom industry oversight is soon to be handed over to anti-monopolies watchdog Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), which has warned it will keep Telstra in check. Telstra held the monopoly over Australia's telecoms system until the industry began to open up five years ago.
Telstra's main rival, Optus Communications, has warned that watchdogs need to be forceful with the state-owned Telstra, otherwise competition will be at risk.
ACCC chairman Allan Fels told the ATUG conference that companies that flout the competition rules will feel the full weight of the commission, once it becomes the industry regulator from July 1.

"If some players, to use a sporting analogy, want to play fast and loose with the rules and engage in unduly rough behaviour, then the umpire will come down extremely hard and fast on such tactics," Fels said.
Optus chief executive officer Zygmunt Switkowski said Telstra needed to toe the line.
"We still have one hugely dominate player and...we will ensure that the player does not use it dominate market position to tilt the playing field," Switkowski said.
"Optus will be very assertive on any examples of what we see as abuse of dominate market position," he told ATUG.

Optus, which was formed under the partial deregulation of the local telecom industry in 1992, is Telstra's only rival in Australia's fixed local telephony and long distance call markets, although resellers have a small presence in the market.

"If we as an industry remain hostage to Telstra's studious ponderous approach to commercial negotiation...and their inherent monopoly endowments then Australia will not get quickly enough the world class telecommunications industry it needs to approach the next decade in the way of nation competiveness," Switkowski said.
Telstra is currently in legal dispute with a serious of competitors including Tasmanian telephone reseller QAI, service providers AAPT Telecommunications and First Netcom.
Both Telstra and Optus plan sharemarket floats later this year. The Australian government hopes to raise at least A$8 billion from the sale of a one third stake in Telstra.
